# How to use this guide

Novel Drug Delivery System is a concept subject: marks come from clear definitions, neat labelled diagrams, classification charts, advantage/disadvantage lists and a few equations. Study one unit a day. Read the notes, then close them and draw each key diagram from memory (reservoir and matrix systems, elementary osmotic pump, buccal patch, transdermal patch layers, floating system, pMDI, liposome, hybridoma flow chart, Ocusert, Copper T). Finish with the question bank and the MCQs for that unit.

The notes follow the five units of the PCI syllabus. Units 2 and 3 each join three short syllabus topics and are written in parts (Part A, B, C) inside one file. The release-kinetics equations (zero order, first order, Higuchi, Korsmeyer–Peppas, Hixson–Crowell) are placed in Unit 1 with the design approaches, because examiners ask them with diffusion and dissolution systems. No unit has been merged or moved.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long (10-mark), short (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions. The very short ones are good warm-ups and help with MCQs.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a diagram or table.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Controlled release and polymers | Definitions (SR, CR, delayed, repeat action), advantages and disadvantages, drug selection, physicochemical and biological properties, diffusion / dissolution / ion-exchange systems, release kinetics equations, classification and applications of polymers |
| 2 Microencapsulation, mucosal, implants | Methods of microencapsulation (coacervation, solvent evaporation, Wurster, spray drying), theories of mucoadhesion, buccal patch formulation, implants, elementary osmotic pump |
| 3 Transdermal, GRDDS, nasopulmonary | Skin permeation and factors, permeation enhancers, components and types of TDDS, approaches to GRDDS (floating, high density, swelling, bioadhesive), pMDI, DPI, nebulisers, nasal sprays |
| 4 Targeted delivery | Levels and approaches of targeting (passive, active, EPR), liposomes (types, preparation, applications), niosomes vs liposomes, nanoparticles, monoclonal antibodies |
| 5 Ocular and intrauterine | Ocular barriers and methods to overcome them, ocular formulations, ocular inserts and Ocusert, IUD generations and mechanism |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Open every answer with a one-line definition, then go to a numbered list or table. "Write a note on" answers should end with applications or examples.
2. Draw a labelled diagram wherever one exists: reservoir vs matrix, osmotic pump, TDDS layers, floating HBS, pMDI, liposome bilayer, Ocusert, Copper T. A neat figure often earns a third of the marks.
3. Give a classification chart at the start of long answers (approaches to CR, methods of microencapsulation, types of TDDS, approaches to GRDDS, types of liposomes, ocular inserts, IUD generations).
4. Learn the equations with the meaning of each symbol: Fick's law, reservoir release dM/dt = ADKΔC/L, Higuchi Q = kH√t, Noyes–Whitney, first-order t1/2 = 0.693/k, Peppas n values, skin flux J = Kp Cv, osmotic pump rate.
5. Practise one numerical: fitting release data to zero order, first order and Higuchi; finding t1/2; calculating flux from a permeability coefficient. Show the formula, substitution and units.
6. Compare-type questions (reservoir vs matrix, liposomes vs niosomes, microcapsules vs microspheres, pMDI vs DPI, buccal vs sublingual, active vs passive targeting) are best answered as a table.
7. Quote named examples for each system (nitroglycerin and scopolamine patches, liposomal doxorubicin, Ocusert pilocarpine, Copper T 380A, push–pull nifedipine system); examiners look for them.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, prepare these with a diagram or table each: **approaches to controlled release with release kinetics**, **methods of microencapsulation**, **mucoadhesion theories and buccal patch**, **elementary osmotic pump**, **transdermal patch components and types**, **approaches to GRDDS**, **pMDI and DPI**, **liposomes**, and **ocular barriers with Ocusert**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Unit 1 — Controlled release and polymers**

| Item | Key facts |
| --- | --- |
| Terms | SR (slow, not constant), CR (predictable, zero order), delayed (enteric), repeat action, targeted |
| Good candidate | t1/2 about 2–8 h, small dose, wide therapeutic index, absorbed throughout gut, stable |
| Reservoir | dM/dt = ADKΔC/L → zero order; risk of dose dumping |
| Matrix | Higuchi Q = kH√t; Q = [D(2A − Cs)Cs t]^½ |
| Dissolution | Noyes–Whitney dC/dt = DA(Cs − C)/h; coated beads of different thickness |
| Ion exchange | Cation resin + basic drug; anion resin + acidic drug; coated complex for SR suspension |
| Kinetics | Zero Q = Q0 + k0t, t1/2 = Q0/2k0; first ln Q = ln Q0 − kt, t1/2 = 0.693/k; Peppas n 0.5 Fickian, 1 case II |
| Polymers | Natural (alginate, chitosan, gelatin), semisynthetic (HPMC, EC, CAP), synthetic (Eudragit, PLGA, EVA, silicone); bulk (PLGA) vs surface (polyanhydride) erosion |
| Eudragit | L >pH 6, S >pH 7, RL/RS insoluble permeable, E dissolves in stomach |

Worked check: 25% released at 1 h by Higuchi → 50% at 4 h, 75% at 9 h; first order k = 0.1 h⁻¹ → t1/2 6.93 h, 70% released in 12 h.

**Unit 2 — Microencapsulation, mucosal, implants**

- Microcapsule = core + wall; microsphere = matrix; 1–1000 µm.
- Coacervation: 3 phases → coacervate deposits → hardening; complex = gelatin + acacia at pH about 4–4.5.
- Others: solvent evaporation (o/w, w/o/w), ionic gelation (alginate + Ca²⁺), interfacial polymerisation, Wurster, pan, spray drying/congealing, multi-orifice centrifugal.
- Mucoadhesion: contact → consolidation; theories: electronic, adsorption, wetting, diffusion, fracture, mechanical. Polymers: carbomer, polycarbophil, CMC, HPMC, chitosan, thiomers.
- Buccal patch: backing (EC) + drug/polymer layer + adhesive; tests: mucoadhesive strength, surface pH, residence time.
- Implants: reservoir (silicone), matrix (EVA rod), biodegradable (PLGA, polyanhydride wafer), pumps, in situ forming.
- EOP: cellulose acetate membrane + drug + osmogen (NaCl) + laser orifice → zero order; push–pull with PEO push layer.

**Unit 3 — Transdermal, GRDDS, nasopulmonary**

- Stratum corneum about 10–20 µm, brick-and-mortar; routes: intercellular (main), transcellular, appendageal.
- J = (DK/h)ΔC = Kp Cv; example Kp 1 × 10⁻³ cm/h, Cv 10 mg/ml → 10 µg/cm²/h.
- Ideal drug: MW below about 500, log P 1–3, low melting point, potent.
- Enhancers: DMSO, azone, PG, ethanol, oleic acid, terpenes, SLS; iontophoresis, electroporation, sonophoresis, microneedles.
- Patch: backing → reservoir/matrix → membrane → PSA → liner. Types: reservoir, drug-in-adhesive, matrix, microreservoir.
- GRDDS: MMC phase III housekeeper wave; floating (HBS, NaHCO3 effervescent, microballoons, rafts), high density >2.5 g/cm³, expandable, inflatable, bioadhesive, magnetic; tests: floating lag time, total floating time.
- Nasal about 150 cm², clearance about 15–20 min; pulmonary 1–5 µm deposit deep; pMDI (HFA-134a/227, oleic acid, ethanol), DPI (lactose carrier), nebulisers (jet, ultrasonic, mesh); cascade impactor.

**Unit 4 — Targeted delivery**

- Levels: organ, cell, intracellular. Passive (RES, EPR), active (ligands), physical, inverse.
- Liposomes: PC + cholesterol; MLV, SUV, LUV; thin-film hydration, sonication, ethanol/ether injection, reverse-phase evaporation, detergent removal; PEGylated doxorubicin, liposomal amphotericin B.
- Niosomes: Span/Tween + cholesterol; cheaper, more stable.
- Nanoparticles: nanospheres, nanocapsules, SLN, NLC; nanoprecipitation, solvent evaporation, ionic gelation; DLS and zeta potential.
- mAbs: hybridoma (myeloma + B cell, PEG fusion, HAT selection); -omab, -ximab, -zumab, -umab; ADCs, immunoliposomes.

**Unit 5 — Ocular and intrauterine**

- Drop 30–50 µl vs cul-de-sac 7–10 µl; tear turnover about 1 µl/min; usually less than about 5% absorbed.
- Cornea: lipophilic epithelium, hydrophilic stroma; blood–aqueous and blood–retinal barriers.
- Fixes: viscosity, gels, in situ gels (CAP latex, poloxamer 407, gellan), mucoadhesives, prodrugs (dipivefrin), cyclodextrins, inserts, intravitreal implants.
- Ocusert: pilocarpine + alginic acid between EVA membranes, TiO2 ring, about a week. Lacrisert: HPC rod for dry eye.
- IUDs: inert (Lippes loop) → copper (Cu-T 380A, Multiload 375) → hormonal (progesterone, levonorgestrel). Action: foreign-body reaction, copper spermicidal, progestogen thickens cervical mucus.

mockTests.title: Full mock paper (75 marks, 3 hours)

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a dosage form that releases drug at a predetermined rate for a set period to keep a nearly constant level in blood or tissue; ideal release is zero order.
2. Terms: sustained release (slow, not necessarily constant), controlled release (predictable, zero order), delayed release (enteric), repeat action, targeted release.
3. Rationale: short half-life drugs need frequent doses; conventional forms cause peaks (near toxic level) and troughs (below MEC); CR keeps the level inside the therapeutic window.
4. Advantages: fewer doses and better compliance; steady levels; fewer peak-related side effects; less total drug; night-time cover; better control of chronic disease; lower overall cost of care.
5. Disadvantages: dose dumping; dose cannot be adjusted or tablet split; drug cannot be removed quickly if toxic; costly; poor IVIVC for some; gut transit limits oral release to 12–24 h.
6. Drug selection: half-life about 2–8 h; small to moderate dose; reasonably wide therapeutic index; good absorption along the whole gut (no narrow window); moderate solubility; stable in gut fluids; low or non-saturable first-pass metabolism; effect related to plasma level.
7. Unsuitable: very short (<1 h) or long (>12 h) half-life, large dose, narrow therapeutic index, absorption window, acid-labile drugs.
8. Diagram: plasma level vs time for conventional (peaks and troughs) and CR (flat line between MEC and MTC).
9. Examples: theophylline, nifedipine, diltiazem, metformin, potassium chloride SR products.
questions.question: Define controlled drug delivery systems. Give the rationale, advantages and disadvantages, and the criteria for selecting a drug candidate for controlled release.

questions.answer:
1. Diffusion follows Fick's first law J = −D dC/dx.
2. Reservoir (membrane) system: drug core inside insoluble membrane (ethyl cellulose, EVA); dM/dt = ADKΔC/L (A area, D diffusion coefficient, K partition coefficient, ΔC concentration difference, L thickness); zero order while core saturated; risk of dose dumping if membrane ruptures; diagram of core + membrane.
3. Matrix (monolithic) system: drug dispersed in polymer (HPMC, EC, wax); release follows Higuchi Q = [D(2A − Cs)Cs t]^½ = kH√t; porous matrix Q = [(Dε/τ)(2A − εCs)Cs t]^½; easy to make, no rupture risk, rate falls with time. Hydrophobic (pores) and hydrophilic (gel layer) matrices.
4. Dissolution-controlled: Noyes–Whitney dC/dt = DA(Cs − C)/h. (a) Encapsulation: beads coated with slowly dissolving coats of different thickness give staggered release. (b) Matrix: drug in slowly dissolving wax or fat; release depends on surface erosion.
5. Combined: insoluble polymer + pore former (EC + HPMC/PEG); pores form and drug diffuses through them.
6. Ion exchange: cross-linked resin with ionisable groups; cation exchanger (–SO3⁻) binds basic drugs, anion exchanger (–NR3⁺) binds acidic drugs; drug released on exchange with Na⁺/Cl⁻ of gut fluid; rate depends on ion concentration, particle size, cross-linking; coating the drug–resin complex with ethyl cellulose gives SR suspensions; also masks taste.
7. Mention others: osmotic pumps, hydrogels, gastroretentive systems.
8. Conclude with a comparison table of release order: reservoir zero, matrix √t, dissolution depends on surface area.
questions.question: Describe diffusion-controlled, dissolution-controlled and ion-exchange approaches to the design of controlled-release formulations with equations and diagrams.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: large molecules made of repeating monomer units; form membranes, matrices, coats and carriers.
2. By origin: natural (gelatin, albumin, alginate, chitosan, starch, guar, xanthan, pectin, hyaluronic acid); semisynthetic (HPMC, MC, EC, Na CMC, cellulose acetate, CAP); synthetic (Eudragit, PVA, PVP, PEG, PLA, PLGA, PCL, polyanhydrides, EVA, silicone, carbomer).
3. By degradation: biodegradable (PLA, PLGA, PCL, polyanhydrides, polyorthoesters, chitosan, gelatin) vs non-biodegradable (EC, EVA, silicone, PMMA).
4. By water interaction: soluble (PEG, PVP), hydrogels (HPMC, pHEMA, carbomer), insoluble (EC, EVA, silicone).
5. By structure: homopolymer, copolymer (random, block, graft); linear, branched, cross-linked. Smart polymers: pH (Eudragit L/S, CAP), temperature (poloxamer 407, PNIPAAm), ions (gellan, alginate).
6. Properties: molecular weight, Tg (glassy vs rubbery), crystallinity, solubility and swelling, permeability, erosion type (bulk PLGA vs surface polyanhydrides), biocompatibility, mechanical strength, film formation, compatibility, cost.
7. Ideal polymer: inert, non-toxic, biocompatible, easy to process and sterilise, gives desired release, stable, safe degradation products, cheap.
8. Advantages: controllable release rate, protection of drug, taste masking, targeting, no removal needed if biodegradable.
9. Applications table: HPMC matrices; EC membranes; Eudragit L/S enteric, RL/RS SR, E taste masking; carbomer mucoadhesive; PLGA microspheres and implants; EVA ocular inserts and rings; silicone implants and IUDs; cellulose acetate osmotic membranes; alginate/chitosan beads and rafts; polyanhydride wafers.
questions.question: Classify polymers used in controlled drug delivery. Discuss their properties, advantages and applications with examples.

questions.answer:
| Point | Sustained release | Controlled release |
|---|---|---|
| Release | Slow, prolonged, often first order | Predetermined, reproducible, ideally zero order |
| Plasma level | Prolonged but not constant | Nearly constant within therapeutic window |
| Control | Mainly duration | Rate and duration (sometimes site) |
| Effect of body | More affected by GI pH, motility | Largely independent of body conditions |
| Examples | Matrix SR tablets | Osmotic pumps, transdermal patches, implants |
Both reduce dosing frequency and improve compliance; all CR products are sustained, but not all SR products are controlled.
questions.question: Differentiate between sustained release and controlled release dosage forms.

questions.answer:
1. Dose size: total dose for the interval must fit one unit; very large doses unsuitable.
2. Aqueous solubility: very low solubility already limits release; very high solubility is hard to slow; solubility changes with pH along the gut.
3. pKa and ionisation: un-ionised form absorbed; pH-dependent solubility gives pH-dependent release.
4. Partition coefficient: moderate log P best; affects diffusion through membranes and polymers.
5. Stability: acid- or enzyme-labile drugs unsuitable for slow release along the gut.
6. Molecular size: diffusivity falls with size; peptides need porous or biodegradable systems.
7. Protein binding: highly bound drugs already long acting.
questions.question: Discuss the physicochemical properties of drugs that influence the design of controlled-release formulations.

questions.answer:
1. Zero order: Q = Q0 + k0t; plot amount released vs t is linear; t1/2 = Q0/2k0; reservoir, osmotic, transdermal systems.
2. First order: ln(100 − Q) = ln100 − k1t; log % remaining vs t linear; t1/2 = 0.693/k1.
3. Higuchi: Q = kH√t (from Q = [D(2A − Cs)Cs t]^½); amount released vs √t linear; matrix systems.
4. Korsmeyer–Peppas: Mt/M∞ = ktⁿ; log–log plot gives n; slab n = 0.5 Fickian, 0.5–1 anomalous, 1 case II (zero order).
5. Data are fitted to each model and the one with highest r² is chosen; n tells the mechanism. Example: data giving r² 0.971 (zero), 0.988 (first), 0.99997 (Higuchi) and n = 0.50 → Fickian diffusion from a matrix.
questions.question: Write the equations for zero-order, first-order and Higuchi release kinetics. How is the release mechanism identified from dissolution data?

questions.answer:
1. Higuchi: Q = kH√t; at 1 h Q = 25%, so kH = 25 % h^−½.
2. At 4 h: Q = 25 × √4 = 50%.
3. At 9 h: Q = 25 × √9 = 75%.
4. Complete release: 100 = 25√t → √t = 4 → t = 16 h.
5. First order: t1/2 = 0.693/k = 0.693/0.1 = 6.93 h; fraction remaining after 12 h = e^(−1.2) = 0.301, so about 70% released.
6. Note: in Higuchi release, four times the time is needed to double the amount released.
questions.question: A matrix tablet releases 25% of its drug in the first hour following Higuchi kinetics. Calculate the percentage released at 4 h and 9 h and the time for complete release. Also find the half-life of a first-order system with k = 0.1 h⁻¹.

questions.answer:
1. Ion-exchange resins: water-insoluble cross-linked polymers with ionisable groups.
2. Cation exchangers (sulfonic acid, –SO3⁻) bind basic drugs; anion exchangers (quaternary ammonium) bind acidic drugs.
3. Release: Resin–SO3⁻ Drug-H⁺ + Na⁺ → Resin–SO3⁻ Na⁺ + Drug-H⁺ (and the anion equivalent with Cl⁻) in gut fluids.
4. Rate depends on ionic strength of fluid, resin particle size, degree of cross-linking, drug loading; not on enzymes.
5. Coated drug–resin complexes (impregnated with PEG then coated with ethyl cellulose, the Pennkinetic approach) give liquid SR suspensions, for example dextromethorphan polistirex.
6. Additional use: taste masking and better stability.
questions.question: Explain the ion-exchange resin approach to controlled release.

questions.answer:
1. Absorption: absorption rate must exceed release rate; drugs with an absorption window in the upper gut are poor candidates for oral CR.
2. Distribution: large Vd and tissue binding influence the amount to be released.
3. Metabolism: saturable first-pass or self-inducing metabolism makes slow input unpredictable.
4. Elimination half-life: ideal about 2–8 h; very short needs too much drug, long gives little benefit.
5. Duration of action: long pharmacological action reduces need for CR.
6. Therapeutic index: narrow index makes dose dumping dangerous.
7. Side effects linked to peaks are reduced by CR.
8. Disease state and circadian rhythm (nocturnal asthma, morning hypertension) may need timed release.
questions.question: Discuss the biological properties of drugs relevant to controlled-release formulations.

questions.answer: The range of plasma concentration between the minimum effective concentration (MEC) and the minimum toxic concentration (MTC); controlled release aims to keep the level within it.
questions.question: Define therapeutic window.

questions.answer: Sudden release of a large part of the drug from a controlled-release product (for example due to a ruptured membrane, chewing or alcohol), which can cause toxicity.
questions.question: What is dose dumping?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: coating of small solids, liquids or gases (core) with a continuous polymer film (wall) to give particles about 1–1000 µm; microcapsules (reservoir) vs microspheres (matrix).
2. Advantages: sustained release, taste masking, liquids to powders, protection from moisture/light/oxygen, less gastric irritation (KCl, aspirin), separation of incompatibles, reduced volatility, depot injections (PLGA), targeting.
3. Coacervation–phase separation: three steps — (i) formation of three immiscible phases (vehicle, core, coating), (ii) deposition of liquid coacervate on core, (iii) rigidisation by heat, cross-linking or desolvation. Induced by temperature change, incompatible polymer, non-solvent, salt (simple coacervation of gelatin with sodium sulfate) or polymer–polymer interaction (complex coacervation of gelatin + acacia at pH about 4–4.5).
4. Solvent evaporation: polymer (PLGA, EC) in volatile solvent (dichloromethane) with drug → emulsified in water with PVA → solvent evaporated → microspheres filtered, washed, dried; w/o/w for water-soluble drugs.
5. Air suspension (Wurster): solid cores fluidised in upward warm air in a vertical chamber; coating sprayed from the bottom of a partition column; particles cycle through spray and drying zones until the desired coat thickness.
6. Diagram of Wurster column and microcapsule vs microsphere.
7. Mention other methods: pan coating, spray drying/congealing, ionic gelation, interfacial polymerisation, multi-orifice centrifugal.
8. Evaluation: yield, size, SEM, encapsulation efficiency, release.
questions.question: Define microencapsulation. Discuss its advantages and describe the coacervation–phase separation, solvent evaporation and air suspension methods of microencapsulation.

questions.answer:
1. Definitions: bioadhesion = attachment to a biological surface; mucoadhesion = attachment to mucus-covered surface. Mucus contains negatively charged mucin glycoproteins.
2. Stages: contact stage (wetting and swelling) and consolidation stage (chain interpenetration, weak bonds).
3. Theories: electronic (electron transfer, double layer), adsorption (H-bonds, van der Waals), wetting (spreading, contact angle), diffusion (interpenetration of chains), fracture (force of separation), mechanical (interlocking in rough surfaces).
4. Factors: polymer molecular weight, chain flexibility, cross-linking, H-bonding groups, concentration, swelling, charge; pH, contact time, applied pressure; mucin turnover and disease.
5. Polymers: carbomer, polycarbophil, Na CMC, sodium alginate, chitosan, HPMC, HPC, PVP; thiomers and lectins.
6. Buccal mucosa: non-keratinised; transcellular and paracellular routes; enhancers (bile salts, SLS, fatty acids, EDTA, cyclodextrins).
7. Ideal drug: small dose, no bitter taste, non-irritant, stable at mouth pH, high first-pass metabolism orally.
8. Buccal patch: backing (EC) + drug/mucoadhesive layer + plasticiser + enhancer; unidirectional release; diagram.
9. Evaluation: thickness, weight, content uniformity, surface pH, swelling, folding endurance, mucoadhesive strength, residence time, in vitro release, ex vivo permeation (Franz cell).
10. Advantages: bypass first-pass, quick removal, local and systemic action; limitations: small area, saliva wash-out, restrictions on eating.
questions.question: What is mucoadhesion? Explain the theories and factors affecting mucoadhesion, and discuss the formulation considerations of buccal drug delivery systems.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: sterile devices placed under skin, in muscle or a body cavity to release drug for weeks to years.
2. Classification: non-biodegradable reservoir (silicone levonorgestrel capsules) and matrix (EVA etonogestrel rod); biodegradable (PLGA goserelin implant, polyanhydride carmustine wafer); pump-type (osmotic — Alzet, DUROS; infusion; vapour pressure); in situ forming implants.
3. Advantages: long action, compliance, no first-pass, local delivery, low dose, removal possible for non-degradable types.
4. Disadvantages: surgery or trocar, pain, infection, migration, no dose change, dose dumping risk, cost, polymer toxicity.
5. Osmotic pump principle: water enters through a semipermeable membrane by osmosis, dissolves drug and osmogen, and the saturated solution is pushed out through an orifice; while solid drug remains, release is zero order.
6. Rate: dM/dt = (Ak/h)(Δπ − ΔP)Cs.
7. Components: drug, osmogen (NaCl, KCl, mannitol), semipermeable membrane (cellulose acetate), plasticiser/flux regulator (PEG), push layer (polyethylene oxide) in push–pull systems, laser-drilled orifice.
8. Types: elementary osmotic pump (water-soluble drugs), push–pull (poorly soluble, nifedipine GITS), implantable Alzet and DUROS.
9. Diagram of EOP.

| Point | Microcapsules | Microspheres |

| Structure | Reservoir: core enclosed in a distinct wall | Matrix: drug dispersed throughout polymer |

| Release | Often zero order through wall | Usually √t (Higuchi) or erosion |
| Risk | Dose dumping if wall breaks | No wall rupture risk |

Both are about 1–1000 µm and are evaluated for size, morphology, entrapment and release.

questions.answer:
1. Phase separation produced by interaction of two oppositely charged colloids.
2. Classic pair: gelatin (positive below its isoelectric point) and gum acacia (negative).
3. Procedure: core dispersed in warm gelatin + acacia solution → pH lowered to about 4–4.5 and diluted with warm water → the two polymers combine to form a coacervate that coats core droplets → cooled to gel the wall → hardened by cross-linking → washed and dried.
4. Used for oils, flavours, vitamins and drugs; also the basis of carbonless copy paper.

questions.answer:
1. Core of water-soluble drug with or without osmogen (NaCl), coated with semipermeable cellulose acetate membrane, with a laser-drilled orifice.
2. Water enters by osmosis, forms saturated solution inside, which is pushed out through the orifice.
3. Release dM/dt = (Ak/h)(Δπ − ΔP)Cs; constant while undissolved drug remains → zero order.
4. Advantages: release independent of pH, food and motility; good IVIVC.
5. Limitations: orifice blockage, mucosal irritation, cost; poorly soluble drugs need push–pull design with polyethylene oxide push layer.
6. Draw labelled diagram.

questions.answer:
1. Electronic theory: electron transfer between polymer and mucus forms a double layer; attraction across it.
2. Adsorption theory: hydrogen bonds, van der Waals and hydrophobic forces after contact.
3. Wetting theory: liquid systems spread on mucus; lower contact angle → better adhesion.
4. Diffusion (interpenetration) theory: polymer and mucin chains diffuse into each other and entangle; depends on chain flexibility and time.
5. Fracture theory: adhesive strength related to force needed to separate the surfaces.
6. Mechanical theory: adhesive fills surface irregularities.
Usually several act together in the contact and consolidation stages.
questions.question: Describe the theories of mucoadhesion.

questions.answer:
Advantages: long duration (weeks to years); better compliance; avoids first-pass metabolism; delivery near the site (carmustine wafer in brain, intravitreal implants); lower total dose; non-biodegradable implants can be removed to stop therapy.
Disadvantages: surgery or trocar insertion; pain, infection, scarring; migration or breakage; dose cannot be changed; possible polymer toxicity; dose dumping from ruptured reservoir; high cost; only potent drugs.
Examples: levonorgestrel silicone capsules, etonogestrel EVA rod, goserelin PLGA implant, DUROS osmotic implant.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: self-contained patches delivering drug through intact skin into systemic circulation at a controlled rate.
2. Skin: stratum corneum (about 10–20 µm, dead corneocytes in lipid — brick and mortar) is the main barrier; viable epidermis; dermis with capillaries.
3. Routes: intercellular (main), transcellular, appendageal (follicles, sweat ducts).
4. Kinetics: Fick's law J = (DK/h)ΔC = Kp Cv; lag time from plot of cumulative amount vs time.
5. Biological factors: skin condition, site, hydration (occlusion), temperature, blood flow, age, metabolism, species.
6. Physicochemical: log P about 1–3, MW below about 500, low melting point, ionisation and vehicle pH, concentration (thermodynamic activity), drug–vehicle interaction.
7. Components: polymer matrix/membrane (EVA, silicone, PIB, HPMC); drug; permeation enhancer; pressure-sensitive adhesive (PIB, acrylates, silicones); backing laminate (polyester, aluminised film); release liner; plasticisers.
8. Diagram of patch layers.
9. Advantages: avoids first-pass, constant input, removable, compliance. Limitations: only potent small drugs, irritation, adhesion problems, slow onset.
10. Examples: nitroglycerin, scopolamine, nicotine, fentanyl, estradiol, clonidine.
questions.question: Define transdermal drug delivery systems. Describe the permeation of drugs through skin, factors affecting permeation and the basic components of TDDS.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: dosage forms retained in the stomach for several hours, releasing drug slowly.
2. Physiology: MMC cycle about 1.5–2 h; phase III housekeeper wave empties stomach in fasting; food delays emptying; pylorus about 12 mm.
3. Suitable drugs: absorption window in upper gut (levodopa, riboflavin, furosemide), local action (antacids, misoprostol, H. pylori therapy), unstable in intestine (captopril), poorly soluble at alkaline pH (diazepam).
4. Floating systems (density below about 1.004 g/cm³): HBS (HPMC gel barrier), effervescent (NaHCO3 + citric acid → CO2), volatile liquid, hollow microspheres, alginate rafts.
5. High-density systems: above about 2.5 g/cm³ with barium sulfate, zinc oxide, iron powder; sit in antrum folds.
6. Expandable/swelling systems: larger than pylorus; superporous hydrogels.
7. Inflatable systems: gas-filled chamber, later deflates.
8. Bioadhesive systems: carbomer, chitosan; limited by mucus turnover.
9. Magnetic systems.
10. Advantages: better bioavailability, local action, fewer doses, less colonic exposure. Disadvantages: need fluid and fed state for floating, variable emptying, unsuitable for irritant or acid-labile drugs, risk of obstruction.
11. Evaluation: floating lag time, total floating time, swelling, density, release, gamma scintigraphy.
12. Diagram of floating HBS.
questions.question: What are gastroretentive drug delivery systems? Discuss the approaches for GRDDS with their advantages, disadvantages and applications.

questions.answer:
1. Nasal route: about 150 cm², rich blood supply; avoids first-pass; rapid onset; peptides (desmopressin, calcitonin) and vaccines; limits — small volume (about 0.1 ml/nostril), mucociliary clearance (about 15–20 min), enzymes, irritation.
2. Pulmonary route: about 70–100 m² alveoli, thin barrier; local therapy in asthma/COPD; deposition by aerodynamic size — above 5 µm impaction in upper airways, 1–5 µm sedimentation in small airways/alveoli, below 1 µm diffusion or exhaled.
3. pMDI: aluminium canister, metering valve, actuator; propellant HFA-134a/HFA-227 (CFCs phased out); surfactant (oleic acid, sorbitan trioleate, lecithin); co-solvent ethanol; micronised drug 1–5 µm; cold or pressure filling; spacers help coordination.
4. DPI: micronised drug + coarse lactose carrier; breath-actuated; unit-dose capsule, multi-unit blister, multi-dose reservoir devices; needs good inspiratory flow; moisture sensitive.
5. Nasal spray: solution/suspension in metered pump; buffer, tonicity agent, preservative (benzalkonium chloride), viscosity agent; tested for dose uniformity, spray pattern, droplet size.
6. Nebulisers: jet (Venturi), ultrasonic (piezoelectric), vibrating mesh; sterile isotonic solutions; useful for children, elderly, acute attacks.
7. Evaluation: delivered dose uniformity, cascade impactor (MMAD, fine particle fraction), leak rate, spray pattern.
8. Diagram of pMDI.
questions.question: Describe nasal and pulmonary routes of drug delivery. Discuss the formulation of metered dose inhalers, dry powder inhalers, nasal sprays and nebulisers.

questions.answer:
1. Agents that reversibly reduce the barrier of stratum corneum to increase drug flux.
2. Chemical: sulfoxides (DMSO), azone (laurocapram), alcohols and glycols (ethanol, propylene glycol), fatty acids (oleic acid), surfactants (SLS, polysorbates), terpenes (menthol, limonene), urea, pyrrolidones, phospholipids.
3. Mechanisms: disrupt intercellular lipids, interact with keratin, improve partitioning of drug into skin.
4. Physical: iontophoresis, electroporation, sonophoresis, microneedles, thermal and laser methods.
5. Ideal: non-toxic, non-irritant, inert, fast and reversible, unidirectional, compatible.
questions.question: What are permeation enhancers? Classify them with examples and mechanisms.

questions.answer:
1. Membrane-moderated reservoir: drug reservoir between backing and rate-controlling membrane (EVA) with adhesive; zero order (nitroglycerin, scopolamine).
2. Adhesive-dispersion (drug-in-adhesive): drug in adhesive layer on backing; thin and simple; may be multilayer (nicotine, estradiol).
3. Matrix diffusion-controlled: drug in polymer disc with peripheral adhesive rim; release ∝ √t.
4. Microreservoir: aqueous drug suspension dispersed as microdroplets in silicone and cross-linked; combines reservoir and matrix.
Preparation by solvent casting, form-fill-seal and lamination.
questions.question: Describe the different types (formulation approaches) of transdermal patches.

questions.answer:
1. Systems with bulk density lower than gastric fluid (about 1.004 g/cm³) that float and stay in the stomach.
2. Non-effervescent: HBS — drug + HPMC in capsule/tablet; outer gel layer, trapped air keeps it buoyant; alginate beads; hollow microspheres; raft-forming alginate liquids.
3. Effervescent: NaHCO3 (± citric acid) produces CO2 trapped in swollen polymer; single, bilayer or multiple-unit; volatile-liquid inflatable systems.
4. Requirements: enough gastric fluid, fed state.
5. Evaluation: floating lag time, total floating time, release.
6. Examples: levodopa–benserazide HBS, diazepam floating capsules, alginate antacid rafts.

questions.question: Compare pressurised metered-dose inhalers and dry powder inhalers.

questions.answer:
1. Devices converting a liquid into a fine mist inhaled over several minutes through mouthpiece or mask.
2. Jet nebuliser: compressed gas through narrow orifice creates low pressure (Venturi/Bernoulli), draws up liquid and breaks it into droplets; baffles remove large droplets.
3. Ultrasonic: piezoelectric crystal vibrates at high frequency to form mist; may heat solution.
4. Vibrating mesh: perforated mesh vibrates and extrudes fine droplets; quiet, portable, little residual volume.
5. Solutions sterile, near isotonic, suitable pH.
6. Advantages: no technique needed, large doses, children/elderly/acute use. Limitations: bulky, slow, need power, dose wastage.

questions.answer:
1. Physiological: mucociliary clearance (about 15–20 min), nasal enzymes, blood flow, disease (cold, allergy).
2. Drug: molecular weight, lipophilicity, ionisation, solubility.
3. Formulation: pH, osmolality, viscosity, droplet/particle size, site of deposition, volume (about 0.1 ml/nostril).
4. Improvement: enhancers (bile salts, surfactants, cyclodextrins, chitosan), enzyme inhibitors, mucoadhesive polymers (carbomer, chitosan) to slow clearance, in situ gels, prodrugs, powder formulations.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: selective delivery of drug to a particular organ, tissue, cell or intracellular site while sparing others; Ehrlich's magic bullet concept.
2. Components: drug + carrier + targeting ligand.
3. Ideal system: selective, protects drug, releases at site, non-toxic, non-immunogenic, biodegradable, stable, easy to make.
4. Levels: first order (organ), second order (specific cells, e.g. tumour cells, Kupffer cells), third order (intracellular, e.g. lysosomes, nucleus).
5. Passive targeting: RES/macrophage uptake of particles >100 nm in liver and spleen; EPR effect in leaky tumour vessels with poor lymph drainage; PEGylated stealth carriers.
6. Active targeting: ligands — antibodies, folate, transferrin, galactose (hepatocytes), mannose (macrophages), RGD peptides.
7. Physical targeting: heat, pH, magnetism, ultrasound, light.
8. Inverse targeting (RES blockade), dual and double targeting.
9. Carriers: liposomes, niosomes, nanoparticles, microspheres, conjugates, resealed erythrocytes, dendrimers, antibodies.
10. Advantages: higher site concentration, less toxicity, lower dose, protection, crossing barriers. Disadvantages: RES clearance, complex and costly, stability problems, immunogenicity, low loading.
questions.question: Define targeted drug delivery. Explain the levels and approaches of drug targeting with their advantages and disadvantages.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: vesicles of one or more concentric phospholipid bilayers enclosing aqueous core; hydrophilic drug in core, lipophilic drug in bilayer; diagram.
2. Composition: phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, PE, PG, DPPC), cholesterol (rigidity, less leakage), charge inducers (stearylamine +, dicetyl phosphate −), PEG-lipids (stealth), antioxidants.
3. Classification by size/lamellarity: MLV (about 0.5–5 µm), SUV (about 20–100 nm), LUV (>100 nm), GUV (>1 µm), multivesicular. By function: conventional, stealth, immunoliposomes, cationic, pH- and thermosensitive.
4. Preparation: thin-film hydration (Bangham) → MLV; sonication → SUV; extrusion through polycarbonate membranes; French press; ethanol/ether injection; reverse-phase evaporation (high entrapment, LUV); detergent removal by dialysis; freeze–thaw.
5. Evaluation: size (DLS), shape and lamellarity (TEM), zeta potential, entrapment efficiency after removal of free drug, release, phase transition (DSC), stability (leakage, oxidation).
6. Applications: PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin (less cardiotoxicity), liposomal amphotericin B (less nephrotoxicity), vaccines, gene delivery, macrophage infections, topical/cosmetic, ocular and pulmonary.
7. Advantages and limitations: biocompatible, carry both drug types, reduce toxicity vs short shelf life, cost, RES uptake, sterilisation difficulty.
questions.question: What are liposomes? Describe their composition, classification, methods of preparation, evaluation and applications.

questions.answer:
(a) Nanoparticles
1. Solid colloidal particles about 10–1000 nm carrying drug.
2. Types: nanospheres (matrix), nanocapsules (reservoir), SLN, NLC, polymeric micelles, dendrimers, gold/silica/iron oxide, albumin-bound.
3. Polymers: PLA, PLGA, PCL, polyalkylcyanoacrylates, chitosan, albumin.
4. Preparation: emulsion–solvent evaporation, nanoprecipitation, salting out, emulsification–diffusion, polymerisation, ionic gelation, high-pressure homogenisation, supercritical fluids.
5. Characterisation: DLS size and PDI, zeta potential, TEM/SEM/AFM, entrapment, release, DSC/XRD.
6. Applications: cancer (EPR), brain delivery, gene/siRNA, vaccines, imaging, theranostics.
(b) Monoclonal antibodies
1. Identical antibodies from one clone binding one epitope.
2. Hybridoma technique (Köhler and Milstein, 1975): immunised mouse B cells + myeloma cells fused with PEG → HAT selection → cloning → production.
3. Types: murine (-omab), chimeric (-ximab: rituximab), humanised (-zumab: trastuzumab), human (-umab: adalimumab).
4. Uses: naked antibodies (trastuzumab HER2, rituximab CD20, bevacizumab VEGF), antibody–drug conjugates (trastuzumab emtansine), radioimmunoconjugates, immunotoxins, immunoliposomes, diagnostics.
5. Limitations: poor tumour penetration, immunogenicity, cost, injection only.
questions.question: Write notes on (a) nanoparticles and (b) monoclonal antibodies in drug delivery.

questions.answer:
| Point | Liposomes | Niosomes |
|---|---|---|
| Bilayer material | Phospholipids + cholesterol | Non-ionic surfactants (Span, Tween, Brij) + cholesterol |
| Chemical stability | Lower (oxidation, hydrolysis) | Higher |
| Cost | High | Low |
| Storage | Special, often under nitrogen | Easier |
| Raw material purity | Variable natural lipids | Uniform synthetic surfactants |
| Use | Marketed medicines (doxorubicin, amphotericin B) | Cosmetics, topical, research |
Both enclose an aqueous core and carry hydrophilic and lipophilic drugs; prepared by similar methods (film hydration, ether injection, reverse-phase evaporation).
questions.question: Differentiate between liposomes and niosomes.

questions.answer:
1. Passive targeting uses natural fate of carriers: uptake of particles by RES macrophages of liver and spleen (useful for leishmaniasis, fungal infections); EPR effect — leaky tumour vessels and poor lymph drainage trap 10–200 nm carriers (PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin).
2. Active targeting attaches ligands to carriers that bind receptors on target cells: antibodies (HER2), folate (folate receptor on cancer cells), transferrin, galactose (hepatocytes), mannose (macrophages), RGD peptides (tumour vessels).
3. Active targeting adds cell selectivity but carriers must first reach the site, often by passive means.
questions.question: Explain passive and active targeting with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Thin-film hydration (Bangham): lipids in chloroform–methanol, evaporated to a film, hydrated with aqueous drug → MLVs.
2. Sonication (probe/bath) of MLVs → SUVs.
3. Extrusion through polycarbonate membranes → uniform LUVs.
4. French pressure cell: high-pressure passage → unilamellar vesicles.
5. Solvent injection: ethanol or ether solution of lipids injected into water.
6. Reverse-phase evaporation: w/o emulsion, solvent removed → gel → LUVs with high entrapment.
7. Detergent removal: mixed micelles dialysed → vesicles.
8. Freeze–thaw and dehydration–rehydration increase entrapment.
questions.question: Describe the methods of preparation of liposomes.

questions.answer:
1. Enhanced permeability and retention effect: passive accumulation of nanocarriers and macromolecules in tumours.
2. Tumour blood vessels are leaky with wide endothelial gaps (enhanced permeability).
3. Tumours have poor lymphatic drainage, so carriers stay (retention).
4. Carriers of roughly 10–200 nm, long-circulating (PEG coated), exploit it.
5. Example: PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin.
6. Limitations: varies between tumours and patients; less in small or poorly vascularised tumours.
questions.question: Write a note on the EPR effect.

questions.answer:
1. Mouse immunised with antigen → spleen B lymphocytes collected.
2. B cells fused with myeloma cells (immortal, non-secreting, HGPRT-deficient) using polyethylene glycol.
3. Cells grown in HAT medium: unfused myeloma cells die, unfused B cells die naturally; only hybridomas survive.
4. Supernatants screened (ELISA) for desired antibody.
5. Positive hybridomas cloned by limiting dilution (single cell).
6. Selected clone grown in bioreactor or culture → antibody purified.
7. Developed by Köhler and Milstein (1975). Mouse antibodies may be chimerised or humanised to reduce immunogenicity.
questions.question: Explain the hybridoma technique for production of monoclonal antibodies.

questions.answer:
Classification: nanospheres (matrix), nanocapsules (reservoir), solid lipid nanoparticles, nanostructured lipid carriers, polymeric micelles, dendrimers, inorganic (gold, silica, iron oxide), protein-based (albumin).
Preparation: emulsion–solvent evaporation; nanoprecipitation (solvent displacement); salting-out; emulsification–solvent diffusion; polymerisation of alkylcyanoacrylates; ionic gelation (chitosan–tripolyphosphate); hot or cold high-pressure homogenisation (SLN, NLC); supercritical fluid methods.
Characterise by DLS, zeta potential, electron microscopy, entrapment efficiency and release.

questions.answer: Blocking the reticuloendothelial system (for example with blank carrier particles) so that a later drug-loaded carrier avoids liver and spleen uptake and reaches other sites.

questions.answer: -ximab: chimeric monoclonal antibody (mouse variable + human constant region), e.g. rituximab; -zumab: humanised antibody, e.g. trastuzumab.

questions.answer:
1. Introduction: eye easy to reach but less than about 5% of an eye drop reaches inner eye.
2. Precorneal barriers: drop 30–50 µl vs cul-de-sac 7–10 µl → overflow and nasolacrimal drainage; tear turnover about 1 µl/min; blinking and reflex tearing; protein binding and tear enzymes; non-productive conjunctival and nasal absorption (systemic side effects).
3. Corneal barrier: lipophilic epithelium with tight junctions, hydrophilic stroma, endothelium → needs balanced log P.
4. Blood–aqueous and blood–retinal barriers limit drug from blood to eye; posterior segment hard to reach.
5. Overcoming: viscosity enhancers (HPMC, PVA); ointments and gels; in situ gels — pH (CAP latex, carbomer), temperature (poloxamer 407), ion (gellan, alginate); mucoadhesives (carbomer, chitosan, hyaluronic acid); prodrugs (dipivefrin, latanoprost); penetration enhancers (BKC, EDTA); cyclodextrins; inserts; colloidal carriers (liposomes, niosomes, nanoparticles); intravitreal injections and implants; iontophoresis; nasolacrimal occlusion.
6. Formulations: solutions, suspensions, emulsions, ointments, gels, inserts, colloidal systems, drug-loaded contact lenses, intravitreal implants.
7. Requirements: sterility, preservative for multidose, pH near 7.4 (tolerated about 6.6–9), isotonic (0.9% NaCl), clarity, fine particle size.
questions.question: Describe the barriers to ocular drug delivery and the methods used to overcome them. Add a note on ocular formulations.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: sterile thin solid or semisolid devices placed in the conjunctival sac to release drug over a long time.
2. Classification: insoluble — diffusion (Ocusert), osmotic, contact lenses; soluble — natural (collagen shields), synthetic/semisynthetic (SODI, Lacrisert HPC rod); bioerodible (poly(orthoesters), cross-linked gelatin).
3. Ocusert: pilocarpine with alginic acid as reservoir sandwiched between two EVA rate-controlling membranes; white titanium dioxide ring for visibility; placed in lower cul-de-sac; releases pilocarpine at nearly constant rate for about one week (glaucoma); diagram.
4. Advantages: prolonged contact and release, accurate dosing, less systemic absorption, zero order possible, no preservative, better stability, fewer applications.
5. Disadvantages: foreign-body sensation, accidental loss, difficult insertion/removal, vision interference, cost.
6. Evaluation: thickness, weight, content uniformity, surface pH, swelling, folding endurance, in vitro release, sterility, irritation tests.
questions.question: Define ocular inserts. Classify them and describe the Ocusert system. Give their advantages and disadvantages.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: small flexible devices inserted into uterus through cervix for long-acting reversible contraception; medicated IUDs release copper or hormones.
2. Development: early rings (Grafenberg); first generation inert plastic (Lippes loop, Margulies coil, Saf-T-coil, with BaSO4 for X-ray visibility); second generation copper (Copper-7, Cu-T 200, Cu-T 380A about 10 years, Multiload Cu-375); third generation hormonal (progesterone IUD about one year, levonorgestrel intrauterine system several years).
3. Design: size/shape to fit cavity and resist expulsion; biocompatible polyethylene/silicone/EVA; copper surface area; steroid reservoir in silicone membrane for near-zero-order release; inserter tube; removal threads; sterile (ethylene oxide).
4. Mechanism: foreign-body inflammatory reaction; copper ions spermicidal; progestogen thickens cervical mucus and thins endometrium.
5. Advantages: long acting, effective, reversible, no daily action, low systemic hormone, reduced menstrual loss with LNG system, cheap, national programme use.
6. Disadvantages: trained insertion, pain and bleeding, expulsion, rare perforation, pelvic infection after insertion, ectopic risk if failure, no STI protection.
7. Applications: contraception, emergency contraception (copper), heavy menstrual bleeding, endometrial protection in HRT.
8. Diagram of Copper T.
questions.question: What are intrauterine devices? Discuss their development, mechanism of action, advantages, disadvantages and applications.

questions.answer:
Precorneal: drop volume (30–50 µl) exceeds cul-de-sac capacity (7–10 µl), so most overflows or drains via nasolacrimal duct; tear turnover about 1 µl/min; blinking and reflex tearing from irritant drops; binding to tear proteins; enzymatic metabolism; conjunctival and nasal absorption into blood.
Corneal: epithelium lipophilic with tight junctions (barrier to hydrophilic drugs); stroma hydrophilic (barrier to very lipophilic drugs); endothelium leaky. Hence drugs with balanced lipophilicity and partial un-ionisation at tear pH penetrate best. Result: usually less than about 5% of the dose enters the eye.
questions.question: Discuss the precorneal and corneal barriers to ocular drug absorption.

questions.answer:
1. Liquids instilled as drops that turn into gels in the eye, increasing contact time without the blur of ointments.
2. pH-triggered: cellulose acetate phthalate latex, carbomer — gel as pH rises to tear pH.
3. Temperature-triggered: poloxamer 407 — gels at eye surface temperature.
4. Ion-activated: gellan gum, sodium alginate — gel with tear cations (Na⁺, Ca²⁺).
5. Advantages: accurate dosing as a drop, prolonged residence, fewer doses, better bioavailability.
6. Evaluation: gelation temperature/pH, viscosity, clarity, sterility, release, irritation.
questions.question: Write a note on in situ gelling ophthalmic systems.

questions.answer:
1. Solubility and need for solubilisers.
2. pKa and partition coefficient to predict corneal penetration.
3. pH–stability and pH–solubility: tear pH about 7.4; tolerated about 6.6–9; weak buffer if drug needs lower pH.
4. Tonicity: isotonic with 0.9% NaCl (tolerated about 0.7–1.5%).
5. Sterility and preservative selection (benzalkonium chloride, chlorobutanol) or preservative-free unit doses.
6. Particle size for suspensions.
7. Viscosity.
8. Container, closure and contact-lens compatibility; ocular irritation.
questions.question: What preliminary (preformulation) studies are carried out for ocular dosage forms?

questions.answer:
1. Early: Grafenberg ring (silk/metal), many complications.
2. First generation (inert): Lippes loop, Margulies coil, Saf-T-coil; polyethylene with BaSO4; larger, more pain and bleeding.
3. Second generation (copper): Copper-7, Cu-T 200, Cu-T 380A (about 10 years), Multiload Cu-375; copper is spermicidal; smaller frames, higher efficacy.
4. Third generation (hormonal): progesterone-releasing IUD (about one year), levonorgestrel intrauterine system (several years); membrane-controlled steroid reservoir; less bleeding; thickens cervical mucus.
questions.question: Describe the generations of intrauterine devices with examples.

questions.answer:
Advantages: longer residence and prolonged release; accurate dosing; reduced systemic absorption; zero-order release possible; no preservatives; better stability; fewer administrations and better compliance.
Disadvantages: foreign-body sensation; may fall out unnoticed; insertion and removal need skill; may disturb vision; higher cost; patient reluctance.
questions.question: Give the advantages and disadvantages of ocular inserts.

questions.answer:
1. Inserts that dissolve in tear fluid, so no removal needed.
2. Natural: collagen shields soaked in drug, dissolve over hours to days.
3. Synthetic/semisynthetic: soluble ophthalmic drug insert (SODI) of polyacrylamide-type polymer; hydroxypropyl cellulose rod (Lacrisert) for dry eye, placed once daily in lower cul-de-sac.
4. Advantages: simple, no removal, prolonged contact.
5. Limitation: release not zero order; may blur vision while dissolving.
questions.question: Write a short note on soluble ocular inserts.

questions.answer: Pilocarpine with alginic acid as the drug reservoir, sandwiched between two ethylene–vinyl acetate rate-controlling membranes, with a titanium dioxide-containing ring for visibility.

questions.answer: Copper ions released into the uterine cavity are spermicidal and add to the local inflammatory reaction, preventing fertilisation.

# Unit 1: Controlled drug delivery systems and polymers

A conventional tablet releases its whole dose at once. Blood levels rise quickly, peak, then fall, so the patient must take another dose a few hours later. Over a day the level swings up and down, sometimes above the safe range and sometimes below the effective range. **Controlled drug delivery** tries to flatten these swings by releasing the drug slowly and at a predictable rate. This unit covers the ideas, the design principles and the polymers used to build such systems.

## 1.1 Introduction and terminology

A **controlled drug delivery system (CDDS)** is a dosage form that releases the drug at a predetermined rate, for a set period, so that a nearly constant drug level is kept in the blood or at the target tissue. The ideal release follows **zero-order kinetics**: the same amount of drug leaves the system every hour, whatever the amount left inside.

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sustained release (SR) | Drug released slowly over a long time; rate is not necessarily constant (often first order) | Matrix SR tablets |
| Controlled release (CR) | Release rate is predictable and reproducible, ideally zero order; the system controls the level in the body | Osmotic pump tablets, transdermal patches |
| Prolonged / extended release (ER, XL) | Gives a longer duration of action than the conventional form; terms often used for SR products | Once-daily ER tablets |
| Delayed release | Release starts only after a lag time or at a chosen site | Enteric-coated tablets |
| Repeat action | Two doses in one unit: one released at once, the second after a delay | Repeat-action tablets with an inner core |
| Site-specific / targeted release | Drug delivered mainly to an organ, tissue or cell | Liposomes, antibody conjugates |
| Receptor targeting | Drug reaches a specific receptor inside the target cell | Ligand-coated nanoparticles |

```text
Plasma level
   |      conventional (each dose)
   | MTC ...../\....../\....../\........  minimum toxic level
   |        /  \    /  \    /  \
   |       /    \  /    \  /    \         controlled release
   |  ----/------\/------\/------\------  ________________
   | MEC /                                 steady level inside window
   |____/__________________________________________ time
        dose 1    dose 2    dose 3
```

The space between the **minimum effective concentration (MEC)** and the **minimum toxic concentration (MTC)** is the **therapeutic window**. A controlled-release product aims to keep the level inside this window for the whole dosing interval.

## 1.2 Rationale, advantages and disadvantages

**Rationale.** Many drugs are cleared quickly, so a conventional form must be taken three or four times a day. Missed doses cause dips below the MEC; large doses cause peaks near the MTC. Controlling the release rate solves both problems.

**Advantages**

1. Fewer doses per day, so better patient compliance (once- or twice-daily dosing).
2. Steadier plasma levels with less "peak and trough" fluctuation.
3. Fewer dose-related side effects (for example less gastric irritation and fewer peak-level effects).
4. Smaller total amount of drug may be needed, since less is wasted at peaks.
5. Night-time dosing is avoided; therapy continues while the patient sleeps.
6. Better control of chronic diseases (hypertension, angina, diabetes, pain).
7. Lower overall health-care cost through better outcomes and fewer visits, despite a higher product cost.

**Disadvantages**

1. **Dose dumping**: if the system fails (for example crushing, chewing or alcohol with some products), a large dose may be released at once.
2. The dose cannot be adjusted easily; tablets usually must not be split.
3. If side effects occur, the drug cannot be removed quickly from the body.
4. More expensive to develop and make.
5. Poor in vitro–in vivo correlation for some products.
6. Gut transit time limits oral systems to about 12–24 hours of release.
7. Unsuitable for drugs with special absorption problems (see selection criteria).

## 1.3 Selection of drug candidates

Not every drug is suitable for controlled release. The general requirements are:

| Property | Suitable | Unsuitable / difficult |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Biological half-life | Short to moderate (roughly 2–8 h) | Very short (under about 1 h: too much drug needed) or long (over about 12 h: already long acting) |
| Dose | Small to moderate | Very large doses (product becomes too big) |
| Therapeutic index | Reasonably wide | Very narrow (dose dumping dangerous) |
| Absorption | Well absorbed along the whole gut | Absorbed only in a narrow "window" in the upper intestine |
| Aqueous solubility | Moderate | Extremely low (release controlled by poor solubility already) |
| Stability | Stable in gut fluids | Unstable in stomach or intestine |
| First-pass metabolism | Low to moderate | Extensive, saturable metabolism (slow input may reduce bioavailability) |
| Mode of action | Effect related to plasma level | Effect not related to level, or tolerance develops with constant levels |

Typical examples of drugs given as SR/CR products are theophylline, diltiazem, nifedipine, metformin, diclofenac, isosorbide mononitrate and potassium chloride.

## 1.4 Physicochemical properties of drugs relevant to controlled release

1. **Dose size.** For oral products the whole dose for the dosing interval must fit in one unit. A very large dose makes the tablet too big to swallow.
2. **Aqueous solubility.** Drugs with very low solubility already dissolve slowly, so their release is limited by dissolution and adding a release barrier gives little benefit. Very soluble drugs are hard to slow down and may need special matrices or coatings. Solubility also changes with pH along the gut, which can change the release rate.
3. **pKa and ionisation.** Only the un-ionised form crosses membranes easily. A drug whose ionisation changes greatly between stomach and intestine may show pH-dependent release and absorption.
4. **Partition coefficient (log P).** Drugs with very high log P stay in membranes and fat; drugs with very low log P cross membranes poorly. A moderate value is best. Log P also affects diffusion through polymer membranes.
5. **Stability.** Drugs unstable in acid (some penicillins) or degraded by intestinal enzymes are poor candidates for systems that release slowly along the gut.
6. **Molecular size and diffusivity.** Diffusion through polymers slows as molecular weight rises. Large molecules such as peptides diffuse very slowly through dense polymers and need porous or biodegradable systems.
7. **Protein binding.** Highly protein-bound drugs already have a long duration of action; binding also affects the free concentration available for effect.

## 1.5 Biological properties of drugs relevant to controlled release

1. **Absorption.** The absorption rate should be faster than the release rate, so that release (not absorption) controls the level. Drugs absorbed only in a short segment of the gut are not good for once-daily oral systems unless the system is held in the stomach (see gastroretentive systems, Unit 3).
2. **Distribution.** A large apparent volume of distribution and slow redistribution affect how much drug must be released.
3. **Metabolism.** Drugs that induce or inhibit their own metabolism, or that undergo saturable first-pass metabolism, behave unpredictably when given slowly.
4. **Elimination half-life.** Decides the release rate needed. Very short half-life drugs need large amounts of drug; long half-life drugs gain little.
5. **Duration of action.** Drugs with long pharmacological action (even with short half-life) may not need CR.
6. **Margin of safety (therapeutic index).** Narrow-index drugs need very reliable release to avoid toxicity.
7. **Side effects.** CR is useful when side effects are linked to peak levels.
8. **Disease state and circadian rhythm.** Some conditions (asthma attacks at night, morning rise in blood pressure) are better treated by timed (chronotherapeutic) release than by a flat level.

## 1.6 Approaches to design controlled-release formulations

```text
Approaches to oral controlled release
├── Diffusion-controlled
│     ├── Reservoir (membrane) systems
│     └── Matrix (monolithic) systems
├── Dissolution-controlled
│     ├── Encapsulation (coated particles)
│     └── Matrix (slowly dissolving)
├── Combined diffusion and dissolution
├── Ion-exchange resin systems
└── Others: osmotic pumps (Unit 2), hydrogels, pH-independent and
            gastroretentive systems (Unit 3)
```

### a. Diffusion-controlled systems

Drug moves from a region of high concentration to low concentration through a polymer. The basic law is **Fick's first law**:

J = −D (dC/dx)

where J is the flux (amount per unit area per unit time), D the diffusion coefficient and dC/dx the concentration gradient.

**1. Reservoir (membrane-controlled) systems.** A core of drug is surrounded by a water-insoluble polymer membrane, for example ethyl cellulose or ethylene–vinyl acetate (EVA).

```text
   ┌──────────────────────┐
   │  rate-controlling    │   membrane (ethyl cellulose, EVA)
   │   ┌──────────────┐   │
   │   │  drug core   │   │   saturated drug solution / solid drug
   │   │ (reservoir)  │   │
   │   └──────────────┘   │
   └──────────────────────┘
        drug diffuses out → constant rate while core stays saturated
```

Release rate: dM/dt = A D K ΔC / L

where A is the area, D the diffusion coefficient in the membrane, K the partition coefficient between membrane and core, ΔC the concentration difference across the membrane and L the membrane thickness. As long as a saturated solution remains inside, ΔC is constant and release is **zero order**. Thicker membrane or lower permeability → slower release.

- Advantages: true zero-order release possible; rate set by the membrane.
- Disadvantages: if the membrane ruptures, the whole dose may be released (dose dumping); harder to make; large molecules diffuse poorly.

**2. Matrix (monolithic) systems.** Drug is dispersed evenly in a polymer matrix (HPMC, ethyl cellulose, waxes). Water enters, dissolves the drug near the surface, and the dissolved drug diffuses out through pores or through the swollen polymer. Drug near the surface leaves first; later drug must travel a longer path, so the rate falls with time. The amount released follows the **Higuchi equation** (square root of time, see 1.7).

- Advantages: easy to make by compression; no risk of dose dumping from a burst membrane.
- Disadvantages: release is not zero order; release rate falls with time.

Matrices may be **hydrophobic / insoluble** (ethyl cellulose, waxes, Eudragit RL/RS: drug leaves through pores) or **hydrophilic / swellable** (HPMC, sodium alginate, xanthan gum: polymer forms a gel layer that slows diffusion and gradually erodes).

### b. Dissolution-controlled systems

Release depends on how fast the drug or its coat dissolves. The **Noyes–Whitney equation** describes dissolution:

dC/dt = D A (Cs − C) / h

where D is the diffusion coefficient, A the surface area, Cs the saturation solubility, C the concentration in bulk solution and h the thickness of the diffusion layer.

1. **Encapsulation (coating) dissolution systems.** Drug particles or pellets are coated with slowly dissolving polymers or waxes of different thickness. Thin coats dissolve early and thick coats later, so the mixture gives a spread of release (the principle of many SR capsules, such as the "spansule" type).
2. **Matrix dissolution systems.** Drug is mixed in a slowly dissolving or eroding material (waxes, fatty acids, hydrogenated oils). Release depends on the rate at which the matrix surface dissolves.

### c. Combined diffusion and dissolution systems

A partly soluble membrane: when the soluble part dissolves, pores form, and drug diffuses through these pores. Example: a coat of ethyl cellulose mixed with a water-soluble polymer (HPMC or PEG) as a pore former.

### d. Ion-exchange resin systems

Ion-exchange resins are water-insoluble cross-linked polymers carrying ionisable groups. Drug ions are bound to the resin and released when they are exchanged for ions of the same charge in the gut fluids.

- **Cation exchange resins** (sulfonic acid groups) bind **basic drugs**: Resin–SO3⁻ Drug-H⁺ + Na⁺ → Resin–SO3⁻ Na⁺ + Drug-H⁺
- **Anion exchange resins** (quaternary ammonium groups) bind **acidic drugs**: Resin–N⁺R3 Drug⁻ + Cl⁻ → Resin–N⁺R3 Cl⁻ + Drug⁻

Release depends on the ion concentration in the fluid, the resin's particle size and cross-linking, not on enzymes or pH alone. To slow release further, the drug–resin complex is coated with a polymer such as ethyl cellulose (the "Pennkinetic" approach, used for liquid SR suspensions such as dextromethorphan polistirex). Resins also mask bitter taste.

## 1.7 Release kinetics: the equations you must know

The way the amount released (Q) changes with time (t) tells us the mechanism. Release data are plotted in different ways, and the plot that gives the straightest line (highest r²) is taken as the best fit.

| Model | Equation | Plot that gives a straight line | Typical system |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zero order | Q = Q0 + k0 t | Amount released vs t | Reservoir, osmotic pump, transdermal patch |
| First order | ln (100 − Q) = ln 100 − k1 t (or log C = log C0 − k t/2.303) | log % remaining vs t | Many SR matrices of soluble drugs |
| Higuchi | Q = kH √t | Amount released vs √t | Matrix (insoluble or porous) systems |
| Korsmeyer–Peppas | Mt/M∞ = k tⁿ | log (Mt/M∞) vs log t | Used to find the mechanism (value of n) |
| Hixson–Crowell | W0^(1/3) − Wt^(1/3) = k t | Cube root of weight remaining vs t | Systems where surface area shrinks as particles dissolve |

**Zero order.** Rate = k0 (a constant). Units of k0: amount per time (mg/h). Half-life t1/2 = Q0/2k0, so it depends on the starting amount.

**First order.** Rate is proportional to the amount left: dQ/dt = −k1 Q. Half-life t1/2 = 0.693/k1, independent of the starting amount. Units of k1: per hour.

**Higuchi model.** For a drug dispersed in a homogeneous matrix:

Q = [D (2A − Cs) Cs t]^½

and for a porous (granular) matrix:

Q = [(D ε / τ) (2A − ε Cs) Cs t]^½

where Q is the amount released per unit area, D the diffusion coefficient, A the total drug loading per unit volume, Cs the drug solubility in the matrix or medium, ε the porosity and τ the tortuosity. Both reduce to Q = kH √t.

**Korsmeyer–Peppas exponent n** (for the first 60% of release, thin film / slab):

| n (slab) | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| 0.5 | Fickian diffusion |
| between 0.5 and 1 | Anomalous (non-Fickian): diffusion plus swelling or erosion |
| 1.0 | Case II transport: polymer relaxation / erosion, giving zero-order release |

For cylinders the Fickian limit is about 0.45, and for spheres about 0.43.

### Worked example 1: zero-order, first-order and Higuchi calculations

1. A reservoir system releases drug at k0 = 5 mg/h. Amount released in 12 h = 5 × 12 = **60 mg** (independent of how much is left, as long as the core is saturated).
2. A matrix tablet releases drug by first-order kinetics with k1 = 0.1 h⁻¹.
   - t1/2 = 0.693/0.1 = **6.93 h**
   - Fraction left after 12 h = e^(−0.1 × 12) = e^(−1.2) = 0.301, so about **70% released**.
3. A matrix releases 25% of its drug in the first hour by Higuchi kinetics (Q = 25√t).
   - At 4 h: 25 × √4 = **50%**; at 9 h: 25 × 3 = **75%**; 100% would need (100/25)² = **16 h**.
   - Notice that doubling the time does not double the release; four times the time doubles it.

### Worked example 2: finding the release model from data

A matrix tablet gave this cumulative release:

| Time (h) | 1 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| % released | 12 | 17 | 24 | 29.5 | 34 | 41.5 |

Linear regression of each plot gives:

| Plot | Slope | r² |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero order (% released vs t) | 2.63 %/h | 0.971 |
| First order (ln % remaining vs t) | −0.0366 h⁻¹ | 0.988 |
| Higuchi (% released vs √t) | 11.99 % per h^½ | 0.99997 |
| Korsmeyer–Peppas (log % vs log t) | n = 0.50 | 0.99998 |

The Higuchi plot is the straightest, and the Peppas exponent n = 0.50 shows **Fickian diffusion** from a matrix. Using Q = 12√t, the time for 60% release would be (60/12)² = **25 h**.

### Worked example 3: design of an oral zero-order product (hypothetical drug)

For a hypothetical drug with elimination rate constant ke = 0.2 h⁻¹, volume of distribution 50 L and a desired steady level of 2 mg/L:

- Required zero-order release rate k0 = ke × Css × Vd = 0.2 × 2 × 50 = **20 mg/h**
- Maintenance amount for 12 h = 20 × 12 = **240 mg**
- Immediate-release (loading) portion Di = Css × Vd = 2 × 50 = **100 mg**
- If the maintenance part already starts releasing at time zero and the peak of the loading portion is at Tp = 1 h, the corrected loading portion Di* = Di − k0 × Tp = 100 − 20 = **80 mg**

These figures are only a teaching example showing how release rate is linked to pharmacokinetics; they are not doses of any real medicine.

## 1.8 Polymers in controlled release

A **polymer** is a large molecule made of many repeating units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds. Polymers form the membranes, matrices, coatings and carriers of almost all novel delivery systems.

### a. Classification

**By origin**

| Class | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Natural | Gelatin, albumin, collagen, sodium alginate, chitosan, starch, guar gum, xanthan gum, gum acacia, pectin, hyaluronic acid |
| Semisynthetic | Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC), methylcellulose, ethyl cellulose, sodium carboxymethylcellulose, cellulose acetate, cellulose acetate phthalate |
| Synthetic | Polymethacrylates (Eudragit), polyvinyl alcohol, polyvinylpyrrolidone, polyethylene glycol, polylactic acid (PLA), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), polycaprolactone, polyanhydrides, ethylene–vinyl acetate, silicone (polydimethylsiloxane), polyacrylic acid (carbomer) |

**By biodegradability**

- **Biodegradable**: broken down in the body to harmless products, so they need not be removed: PLA, PLGA, polycaprolactone, polyanhydrides, polyorthoesters, chitosan, albumin, gelatin.
- **Non-biodegradable**: stay intact and must be removed or excreted unchanged: ethyl cellulose, EVA, silicone rubber, polyurethanes, polymethyl methacrylate.

**By interaction with water**

- Hydrophilic / water-soluble (PEG, PVP, HPMC).
- Hydrogels: swell in water without dissolving (cross-linked HPMC, polyhydroxyethyl methacrylate, carbomer).
- Hydrophobic / water-insoluble (ethyl cellulose, EVA, silicone).

**By structure**: homopolymer (one monomer) and copolymer (two or more monomers: random, block, graft, alternating); linear, branched or cross-linked.

**Smart (stimuli-responsive) polymers** change their properties with pH, temperature, ions or enzymes:

| Stimulus | Example polymer | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pH | Eudragit L100 (dissolves above about pH 6), Eudragit S100 (above about pH 7), cellulose acetate phthalate | Enteric and colon delivery |
| Temperature | Poloxamer 407, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) | In situ gels |
| Ions | Gellan gum, sodium alginate (gel with Ca²⁺) | Ophthalmic in situ gels, rafts |

### b. Properties that matter

1. **Molecular weight and its distribution**: higher molecular weight → more viscous gels, slower diffusion and slower erosion.
2. **Glass transition temperature (Tg)**: below Tg the polymer is glassy and rigid; above it, rubbery and more permeable. Plasticisers lower Tg.
3. **Crystallinity**: crystalline regions are impermeable; drug diffuses through amorphous regions.
4. **Solubility and swelling** in water and at different pH values.
5. **Permeability** to the drug and to water.
6. **Degradation**: **bulk erosion** (water enters the whole mass, which degrades throughout, as with PLGA) or **surface erosion** (only the surface wears away, as with polyanhydrides, giving release nearer zero order).
7. **Biocompatibility and safety**: non-toxic, non-irritant, non-carcinogenic; degradation products safe.
8. **Mechanical strength, film-forming ability and processability.**
9. **Compatibility** with the drug and other excipients; stability; cost and availability.

### c. Ideal properties of a polymer for drug delivery

- Inert and compatible with the drug.
- Non-toxic, biocompatible and free of leachable impurities.
- Easy to make, sterilise and process into the needed shape.
- Allows the desired release rate with a wide range of drugs.
- Stable during storage; good mechanical strength.
- If biodegradable, degrades at a predictable rate to safe products.
- Inexpensive and available in consistent quality.

### d. Advantages of polymers in controlled release

- Release rate can be controlled by choosing polymer type, grade, amount and thickness.
- Protect drug from the environment (moisture, acid, enzymes).
- Mask taste and reduce irritation.
- Allow targeting (enteric, colon, mucoadhesive, tumour-seeking carriers).
- Biodegradable polymers avoid surgical removal of implants.

### e. Applications

| Polymer | Application |
| --- | --- |
| HPMC | Hydrophilic matrix tablets, film coating, ophthalmic solutions |
| Ethyl cellulose | Insoluble membrane coatings, matrix tablets, microcapsule walls |
| Eudragit L, S | Enteric and colon-targeted coatings |
| Eudragit RL, RS | Insoluble but permeable SR coatings (RL high, RS low permeability) |
| Eudragit E | Coating that dissolves in stomach acid; taste masking |
| Carbomer, polycarbophil | Mucoadhesive buccal and vaginal systems |
| PLGA, PLA | Biodegradable microspheres and implants for injections lasting weeks to months |
| EVA | Rate-controlling membranes (ocular inserts, contraceptive vaginal rings, implants) |
| Silicone | Implants, transdermal adhesives, intrauterine devices |
| Cellulose acetate | Semipermeable membrane of osmotic pumps |
| Sodium alginate, chitosan | Microspheres, raft-forming and floating systems, nanoparticles |
| Polyanhydrides | Surface-eroding implant wafers |

## Remember

- CR = predetermined, ideally zero-order release that keeps the level within the therapeutic window; SR = slow release, not necessarily constant.
- Good candidates: half-life about 2–8 h, small dose, wide therapeutic index, good absorption throughout the gut, stable in gut fluids.
- Reservoir: dM/dt = ADKΔC/L, zero order while the core is saturated, risk of dose dumping. Matrix: Higuchi Q = kH√t.
- Noyes–Whitney: dC/dt = DA(Cs − C)/h for dissolution-controlled systems.
- First-order t1/2 = 0.693/k; zero-order t1/2 = Q0/2k0.
- Peppas n (slab): 0.5 Fickian, 0.5–1 anomalous, 1 case II (zero order).
- Cation exchangers carry basic drugs; anion exchangers carry acidic drugs; coated drug–resin complexes give SR suspensions.
- Polymers: natural, semisynthetic, synthetic; biodegradable (PLGA, PLA, polyanhydrides) vs non-biodegradable (EVA, silicone, ethyl cellulose); bulk vs surface erosion.
